questions.subject: en
questions.passage: When companies first sent their staff home to work, many managers expected productivity to fall. In many cases the opposite happened. Without long commutes, employees had more time and energy, and some reported finishing tasks faster in a quiet home environment. Yet remote work has a less visible cost. Younger workers, in particular, say they learn less because they cannot simply watch and ask experienced colleagues. Casual conversations by the coffee machine, which often produce new ideas, have largely disappeared. As a result, a growing number of firms now ask employees to come to the office two or three days a week, hoping to keep the benefits of both worlds.
questions.text: What did many managers expect when staff started working from home?

questions.subject: en
questions.passage: On a summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees hotter than the countryside around it. This effect is known as an urban heat island. Concrete, asphalt and dark roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release the heat slowly at night, so cities cool down far less than rural areas. Cars, air conditioners and factories add even more heat. The consequences are serious: higher energy bills, poorer air quality and greater health risks for elderly people. Fortunately, there are solutions. Planting trees, creating parks and painting roofs in light colours can noticeably reduce temperatures, while green roofs covered with plants also help to absorb rainwater.
questions.text: What is an urban heat island?
options: a cold area in a city
an island in a hot sea
a park in the city centre
a city area that is hotter than the countryside around it

questions.subject: en
questions.passage: Kamran had practised the violin piece for months, but as he waited behind the curtain, his hands were shaking. He could hear the audience whispering and imagined every possible mistake. His teacher noticed his face and quietly told him to breathe slowly and to focus on the first four notes only — not on the whole performance. When Kamran stepped onto the stage, he followed her advice. The first notes sounded weak, but gradually his confidence returned. He made one small mistake in the middle, yet he kept playing. When he finished, the hall burst into applause. Later he admitted that the mistake had taught him something: a performance does not need to be perfect to move people.
questions.text: How did Kamran feel before the performance?

questions.subject: en
questions.passage: For more than a thousand years, the network of trade routes known as the Silk Road connected China with the Mediterranean. Merchants carried silk, spices, paper and porcelain westwards, while glassware, wool and precious metals travelled east. Few traders crossed the entire route; instead, goods passed from hand to hand through many cities. Along the way, caravanserais — roadside inns with rooms for travellers and space for their animals — offered shelter and safety. However, the Silk Road was not only about goods. Religions, languages, scientific knowledge and even recipes spread along it, which is why historians often describe it as one of the first great channels of cultural exchange.
questions.text: What did the Silk Road connect?

questions.subject: en
questions.passage: Every day, millions of people share news stories online without checking whether they are true. False information often spreads faster than accurate reports because it is designed to provoke strong emotions such as fear or anger. Experts recommend a few simple habits. First, check who published the story and whether the source is known for reliable reporting. Second, look for the same news on other trusted websites. Third, pay attention to the date: old stories are sometimes shared as if they were new. Finally, be suspicious of headlines that seem too shocking to be true. Taking thirty seconds to think before sharing can stop a false story from reaching thousands of people.
questions.text: Why does false information often spread quickly?
options: It is designed to provoke strong emotions.
questions.explanation: «…designed to provoke strong emotions such as fear or anger.»

questions.subject: en
questions.passage: It is commonly believed that children learn foreign languages more easily than adults. In some ways this is true: young children often develop a more natural accent. However, research suggests that adults have important advantages too. They can understand grammar rules more quickly, use learning strategies consciously and connect new words to knowledge they already have. The main obstacles for adult learners are often not biological but practical: lack of time, fear of making mistakes and fewer chances to practise. Teachers therefore advise adults to set small, regular goals, to accept errors as part of learning and to find real situations in which to use the language.
questions.text: In what way do children have an advantage, according to the text?
options: They often develop a more natural accent.
